title: The Windrush Generation
author: Latoyah Innerarity
note: Pages received so far (transcribed from screenshots, 6 Oct 2026). Waiting for pages 10–14.

pages.heading: The Voyage of a Lifetime
pages.text: It was 1948 and the HMT (His Majesty’s Transport) Windrush ship was perched on the Jamaican coast of Kingston as passengers from all over the island queued for the voyage of a lifetime – to start a new life in England. The queue, made up of mostly men and some women and children, were dressed in their finest clothes and as they waited to board, they chatted excitedly about the trip that would change their lives. Lasting a total of 22 days, and costing the passengers an expensive £28, (equivalent to £850 in today’s money) the ship sailed across the Caribbean Sea, stopping for passengers from neighbouring islands, before heading 8,000 miles across the Atlantic Ocean to England.

pages.heading: Arrival
pages.text: It was a lively journey, the ship buzzing with the sound of calypso music and the slam of dominos on the table, and when it reached its final destination: the dock at Tilbury, Essex, the media were waiting to capture the ship’s historic arrival. This incredible journey is the story of Caribbean immigration to the UK. Where hundreds of Caribbean people left their families, friends and their sunny islands to live somewhere completely different - a land of fish and chips, cups of tea and lots of rain! It was also a journey that marked the start of a cultural shift in Great Britain that eventually turned the country into a more diverse and accepting place.

pages.heading: Why England?
pages.text: At the end of World War II, Britain was left devastated by German bombings which had destroyed many cities, homes and public buildings. The country needed to be rebuilt but there weren’t enough workers to do the job. There were also shortages in the postal and transportation services and the new National Health Service. Unfortunately, much of Britain’s working population - those strong and healthy enough to work, had either died in the war or were injured. Others were moving to newly established Commonwealth countries Australia, Canada and New Zealand, which were un-affected by the war.

pages.heading: Workers Wanted
pages.text: Britain needed to find workers elsewhere so they requested help from countries in the British Empire (other nations around the world that Britain ruled). This included the Caribbean islands of Barbados, Trinidad, the Bahamas and Jamaica. To make it easier for people to move, the government passed the Nationality Act in 1948, which allowed people from British colonies the legal right to live and work in England. Adverts were placed in newspapers across the Caribbean colonies which promised those willing to leave the islands plenty of job opportunities, places to live and good wages in England.

pages.heading: Jamaica
pages.text: Although many countries had either seen the advert or had heard about it on the radio or through their government, the largest response came from the Caribbean island of Jamaica. In the 1940s, Jamaica was experiencing high rates of unemployment, made worse by a recent hurricane which had ruined much of its farm land. Britain needed workers and Jamaicans needed jobs. At the time, many Caribbean people fondly considered Britain to be their ‘motherland.’ They respected England and thought they would be welcomed there as members of the British Empire. This made them excited to come to England and many aspired to educate their children there, buy a home and start their own businesses.

pages.heading: Life in England
pages.text: Life in England was not what the Windrush arrivals had hoped for. They found themselves unprepared for how cold it was. Although they arrived in the summer, it was a cool summer and many realised the clothes they had packed weren’t warm enough. The poverty in England was another surprise. At the time, England had the largest empire in the world and was considered a powerful and wealthy nation. Caribbean radio programmes also portrayed England as a superior country without the troubles the islands faced. For the Windrush passengers, who were expecting clean streets and lovely houses, it was a shock arriving in England. It was shabby, dirty and food was still being rationed. Many passengers even wondered if they were in the right country.

pages.heading: An Unkind Welcome
pages.text: An even bigger disappointment was the English public’s response to their arrival. Instead of the warm welcome they imagined, the Windrush passengers sadly encountered racism, insults and violence. Places where the arrivals socialised were set on fire or had bricks thrown through the windows. In the streets they were sometimes spat at and called rude names. Some shops and restaurants refused to serve them, and they were even denied entry to some churches.

pages.heading: Early Struggles
pages.text: Despite being promised jobs and places to live, the reality was much different. A lot of British people didn’t want to employ black people and if they did, they were paid less than white people. Although many of the Windrush arrivals were skilled professionals – some were mechanics, teachers, dressmakers, musicians and carpenters - they were forced to accept menial (unskilled) jobs they were over-qualified for. Some people even had to work two jobs to make the money they needed to survive.

pages.heading: Discrimination
pages.text: Housing was also a struggle as many landlords didn’t want to rent their homes to black people and some landlords exploited the Windrush arrivals by renting them over-priced and overcrowded accommodation. The government stepped in to provide un-used air aid shelters for those unable to find homes. However, these were cold, dirty, overcrowded and with minimal facilities like toilets, bathrooms and places to cook. Banking was another challenge for the Windrush arrivals as they were often denied loans, mortgages and even bank accounts. This made it difficult to achieve the aspirations they had back in the Caribbean, such as starting a business, buying a home and sending money to their families back in the Caribbean.
